claims.text: Selective oxidation of Cr governs the formation and persistence of a protective oxide layer in CrFeCoNiX alloys above 900 °C.
Selective Cr oxidation forms a dense, adherent, Cr-rich oxide scale.
Adding Si, Mn, or Al enhances Cr-rich scale stability by modifying interfacial stresses and oxide-growth kinetics.
The initial CrFeCoNiX alloys have a uniform elemental distribution in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state.
Exposure above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere produces a coherent Cr-rich oxide layer.
The X element mitigates oxide-scale interfacial stress by changing lattice parameters or defect chemistry.
The Cr-rich oxide layer is slow-growing and dense.
Si, Mn, or Al segregates to the oxide–matrix interface or enters the oxide lattice.
Interfacial segregation or lattice incorporation of X reduces thermal and growth-induced stresses that would otherwise cause cracking or spallation.
X-induced changes in oxide-growth kinetics improve scale adhesion and continuity.
CrFeCoNiX samples will form a more uniform and adherent Cr-rich oxide layer than CrFeCoNi samples under identical exposure conditions.
CrFeCoNiX samples will exhibit slower oxide growth, lower crack density, and less spallation than the CrFeCoNi baseline.
The oxide scale on CrFeCoNiX will retain continuity and barrier functionality throughout prolonged high-temperature exposure.
CrFeCoNi without X forms less stable, more crack-prone, and more spallation-susceptible oxide scales under the same exposure conditions.
Differences between single- and multiphase states may affect element partitioning and high-temperature diffusion kinetics.
